title: Chapter 84 — Pitchpoling
paragraphs: To make them run easily and swiftly, the axles of carriages are anointed; and for much the same purpose, some whalers perform a similar operation on their boats — they grease the bottom. Nor can it be doubted that, since such a procedure can do no harm, it may possibly be of no small advantage, considering that oil and water are hostile, that oil is a sliding thing, and that the object in view is to make the boat slide bravely along. Queequeg believed strongly in anointing his boat, and one morning, not long after the German ship Jungfrau disappeared, he took more than his usual pains over it, crawling under its bottom where it hung over the side and rubbing in the grease as though he were diligently trying to raise a crop of hair on the craft's bald keel. He seemed to be acting on some particular premonition. Nor did what followed prove it unfounded.
Toward noon whales were sighted; but as soon as the ship sailed down on them, they turned and fled in headlong haste — a disordered flight, like that of Cleopatra's barges from Actium.

Nevertheless, the boats gave chase, and Stubb's was in the lead. With great effort, Tashtego at last managed to plant one iron; but the stricken whale, without sounding at all, kept up his horizontal flight, even faster than before. Such unbroken strain on the planted iron must sooner or later inevitably pull it out. It became essential to lance the fleeing whale, or be content to lose him. But hauling the boat up to his flank was impossible; he swam so fast and furiously. What was left, then?

Of all the wondrous devices and skills, the sleights of hand and countless subtleties that the veteran whaleman is so often driven to, none surpass that fine maneuver with the lance called pitchpoling. Neither small sword nor broadsword, in all its drills, can boast anything like it. It is indispensable only with a whale that is a stubborn runner; its great feature and fact is the wonderful distance to which the long lance is accurately thrown from a violently rocking, jerking boat racing ahead at full speed. Steel and wood included, the whole spear is some ten or twelve feet long; the shaft is much slighter than the harpoon's, and of a lighter material too — pine. It is fitted with a small rope of considerable length, called a warp, by which it can be hauled back to the hand after the throw.

But before going further, it is important to mention here that although the harpoon may be pitchpoled in the same way as the lance, it is seldom done; and when it is, it succeeds still less often, because of the harpoon's greater weight and shorter length compared with the lance, which in practice become serious drawbacks. As a general rule, therefore, you must first get fast to a whale before any pitchpoling comes into play.

Look now at Stubb — a man whose humorous, deliberate coolness and composure in the direst emergencies made him especially fit to excel at pitchpoling. Look at him: he stands upright in the tossing bow of the flying boat; wrapped in fleecy foam, the towing whale is forty feet ahead. Handling the long lance lightly, glancing two or three times along its length to see that it is exactly straight, Stubb, whistling, gathers up the coil of the warp in one hand, so as to keep its free end in his grip and leave the rest unobstructed. Then, holding the lance squarely in front of the middle of his waistband, he levels it at the whale; and, keeping it trained on him, he steadily presses down the butt-end in his hand, thereby raising the point until the weapon stands neatly balanced on his palm, fifteen feet in the air. He reminds you a little of a juggler balancing a long staff on his chin. The next moment, with a rapid, nameless impulse, the bright steel spans the foaming distance in a superb, lofty arc and quivers in the whale's life-spot. Instead of sparkling water, he now spouts red blood.

"That drove the spigot out of him!" cried Stubb. "It's the immortal Fourth of July; all fountains must run wine today! If only it were old Orleans whiskey, or old Ohio, or unspeakable old Monongahela! Then, Tashtego, lad, I'd have you hold a mug to the jet, and we'd drink a round from it! Yes, truly, my hearties, we'd brew choice punch in the spread of his spout-hole there, and from that live punch-bowl drink down the living stuff."

Again and again, to such playful talk, the deft throw is repeated, the spear returning to its master like a greyhound held on a skillful leash. The agonized whale goes into his flurry, the convulsion of his death; the towline is slackened, and the pitchpoler, dropping astern, folds his hands and silently watches the monster die.
